    Advancing Energy Technology
    The global shift toward electrification, automation and digitalization is
    reshaping every segment in which we operate. By advancing Energy Tech to
    the next level of Intelligence, we drive innovation that enables smarter, more
    efficient, and more resilient systems. Focused on technology leadership,
    customer differentiation and operational excellence, we are positioned
    to deliver sustainable growth and long-term value.


    Three mega-trends impacting our market
    Three major mega-trends are reshaping the global landscape: the accelerating shift toward electrification and digitalization; the rapid rise
    of artificial intelligence across personal and industrial domains; and the emergence of a more decentralized, multipolar world. Electrification
    is expanding across sectors and driving more efficient, ﬂexible, and distributed energy architectures, while Digitalization & AI is creating
    unprecedented compute needs. At the same time, geopolitical fragmentation is prompting re-shoring, localized investments, and greater
    focus on technological and cloud sovereignty, bringing both new opportunities and added complexity.



      1. New Energy Landscape                                   2. Digitalization & AI                     3. Multi-Polar World


           See Chapter 1 on page 51 to find out more.




    Energy Tech as a catalyst to drive market growth opportunities
    The end markets we serve remain in an accelerated growth phase as a function of the three mega-trends. Our addressable market
    is set to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of between +6% and +7% between 2025 and 2030, to reach in excess of
    around EUR 600 billion by 2030.

     Data Center & Networks end market
     Digitalization and AI mega-trends are driving unprecedented changes and opportunities to the Data Center &
     Networks end market with increased needs for both Energy Management and software offers. Strong future
     growth is expected, with critical needs for electrical content and cooling boosted by this turning point in
     technology. Through our best-in-class electrification and liquid cooling portfolio, reinforced by the
     acquisition of Motivair, we help data centers design, build, operate, and maintain highly efficient and
     resilient AI-ready infrastructure across the entire lifecycle.

Buildings end market

                                                                                                                                    I N T E G R AT E D R E P O R T
Strong mega-trends are driving growth for the Buildings end market. On one hand, the growing population
and increasing urbanization in emerging economies is driving the need for construction with a rise in
first time demand together with increased digitalization. On the other hand, there is a need for existing
infrastructure refresh, particularly in mature economies where radical acceleration with retrofit is required
in order to meet decarbonization commitments, supported by government investment.

     Industry end market
     Within the Industry end market we target electro-intensive industrial companies in multiple segments including
     Energies & Chemicals, Consumer Packaged Goods, and OEMs. We bring our complementary Energy
     Management and Industrial Automation offers together to fulfill the needs for energy efficiency, increased
     automation, and sustainability. The Industry end market is driven by the acceleration of digitalization and
     process electrification coupled with trends of reshoring and supply chain resilience.

Infrastructure end market

                                                                                                                                    I N T E G R AT E D R E P O R T
Within the infrastructure end market we primarily address the needs from grid, transportation and water and
wastewater segments. The grid is going through a structural transformation as it represents a bottleneck to
the energy transition. Increased power requirement, resiliency, and safety needs are driving investments
around grid modernization, grid extension for extended power reach, and grid digitalization for increased
efficiency and sustainability.

     Digital update
     In 2025, the Digital Flywheel represented 62% of Group revenues (vs. 57% in 2024), showing strong progress towards a target of >70% by
     2030, growing at +15% in 2025. All four elements of the Digital Flywheel made a strong contribution to the growth, led by Connectable
     Products as the Group continues to generate value for customers through the digitalization of its product offering, as a foundation for
     Advancing Energy Tech. Overall, Software & Services represented 19% of Group revenues in 2025, with an ambition for this representation
     to reach c.25% by 2030. Digital Services grew strongly, while the Group’s agnostic software offers also made a strong contribution despite
     their ongoing transition to a subscription model. Recurring revenues within agnostic software increased to 79% (vs. 77% in 2024), led by
     AVEVA, which achieved close to 85% as outlined in the Group’s 2025 Capital Markets Day. The Group aims to double the weightage of
     total recurring revenues by 2030.

Our Enterprise Risk Management




                                                                                                                                                                           I N T E G R AT E D R E P O R T
Schneider Electric places a significant importance on resilience within the values and principles which guide its actions, as a key element
for sustainable growth which is part of the Group’s Sustainability value.


An Enterprise Risk Management based on the three lines of defense model
Schneider Electric uses a hybrid risk management model with central functions and experts in charge of setting risk management
mechanisms, establishing policies, and other activities, while the ownership of the risks belongs to the Business Units, Operating Divisions,
or Global Functions who are responsible for deploying the central framework to manage their risks.


                                                               Board of Directors                                                                                          CH1
    Accountable to stakeholders for organizational oversight. The Board is informed about the efficiency of the internal control and risk management systems.


                                                                                                                                                                           CH2

     Schneider Electric’s vigilance plan
     Schneider Electric started in 2017 the implementation of a vigilance plan covering its business activities
     as well as those of its suppliers and subcontractors in order to prevent negative impacts on people or
     the planet within its value chain. Since then, this vigilance plan has been continuously reinforced,
     aiming to expand further towards communities.

     An end-to-end, risk-based mitigation plan
     The Group’s vigilance plan complies with the provisions of the 2017 French law on corporate duty of vigilance and includes:
     • A risk analysis specific to risks that Schneider Electric poses or may pose on its ecosystem and environment;
     • A review of the key actions implemented to remediate or mitigate these risks;
     • An alert system (Trust Line); and
     • Governance specific to vigilance.

     In this Universal Registration document, Schneider Electric presents the results of the risk assessment, and the subsequent mitigation
     actions. A synthesis of key risks and actions is presented below.
     The plan is governed by the Duty of Vigilance Committee, set up in 2017. The committee meets twice a year, and has met 19 times since its inception.

progress against its sustainability goals with a unique
transformation dashboard today called Schneider Sustainability
Impact (SSI).

into 11 highly transformative and innovative programs, executing           1. Focused

     Impact starts with us
     The world is transforming at an unprecedented speed and there is a greater need for us at Schneider Electric
     to play to the emerging opportunities. “Impact starts with us” is a promise the company makes to each of its
     employees, and it is also an invitation for outside talent to join the Company and make an impact on the
     world we share.

     Our Culture                                                               Leadership
     2025 was a pivotal year for Schneider Electric as the Group               Schneider Electric’s leaders play a critical role, as they are the
     advanced its strategic program and accelerated cultural                   architects of the Group’s business and culture. They drive this
     transformation. Its ambition is clear: to build a culture anchored        transformation through the IMPACT Leader Code, which
     in performance, simplicity, and speed, always with people at the          emphasizes inventing the future, delivering the mission together,
     center of everything that is undertaken. This cultural evolution          and building great teams. By living these commitments, Schneider

     Culture is the foundation of how Schneider operates and
     succeeds. It defines how the Group leads, collaborates, and
     innovates. At Schneider Electric, every aspect of its work – from
     how it interacts with customers to how it makes decisions – is
     shaped by its shared IMPACT Values and Leader Code
     commitments.

     IMPACT Values
     Values anchor the way collaborators work at Schneider Electric
     and help bring its growth culture and Employee Value Proposition
     promise to life. Schneider’s six IMPACT Values are derived from its
     ambitions, People Strategy, and the voice of its employees and
     customers:
     • Inclusion: We embrace diverse perspectives, co-creating a
       place where everyone belongs and thrives.
     • Mastery: We count on our expertise and know-how to deliver the
       highest quality innovations.
     • Purpose: We aspire to build a sustainable future for our people,
       customers, communities, and planet.
     • Action: We get things done with accountability, speed and
       integrity, always with the customer in mind.
     • Curiosity: We love to think deeply and differently, challenging
       the status quo and learning every day.
     • Teamwork: We achieve together with our teams, collaborating
       with trust and openness.

     Chapter 1 – Group strategy
     1.1 Strategy Overview



     1.1 Strategy Overview
     We are living through a time of profound global transformation shaped by unprecedented technological,
     environmental, and geopolitical forces. The pressures acting upon our civil infrastructure, energy
     systems, and supply chains impact all aspects of society and the global economy. These aren’t just
     disruptions to manage, but signals that our industry must evolve.
     Three “mega-trends” are accelerating and shaping our end markets over the next decade: acceleration of the New Energy Landscape,
     rapid development and adoption of Digitalization and AI technologies, and a shift towards a Multi-Polar World. Studying these trends has
     allowed us to sharpen the focus of our mission. At this critical moment, we want to be the company that advances energy technology; the
     company which will electrify, automate and digitalize every industry, business, and home, driving efficiency and sustainability for all.

     The portfolio we have created combines energy management, industrial automation, and software capabilities to deliver unique value
     across our four end markets. It facilitates the realization of our mission by laying the foundation for digital innovation with seamlessly
     integrated data center power, cooling, software, and services. It also unifies building systems for smarter, faster decision-making;
     transforming industries, from Food and Beverage and Life Sciences to critical infrastructure and process operations, with open, software-
     defined automation. In addition, it deploys resilient and scalable electrification for grids, mobility, and semiconductor industries.

     In this period, there is both challenge and opportunity. The challenge is great, but the opportunity is even greater. Our energy technology
     enables our partners, customers, and industry to not just adapt, but to thrive in this new era. Schneider Electric doesn’t react to change,

There is no shortage of predictions on how the world will evolve over the next decade, Schneider
Electric has focused on those market signals that have the greatest potential to inﬂuence our operating
environment and our strategic priorities.
A “mega-trend” is a long-term pattern that will have significant impact on all aspects of society and the global economy. In the context of
Schneider Electric, we use mega-trend analysis to develop our corporate, business unit, and zone strategies. They account for a wide
range of factors, including political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental.

partnerships with industry leaders such as NVIDIA ensure our customers can deploy advanced AI clusters reliably.

The solutions to make homes future-ready exist today. Home Energy Management Solutions (HEMS) are powered by AI to efficiently
manage energy production, storage, and consumption. Homeowners can control energy use and costs, reduce carbon emissions, and
even generate, store, and sell electricity while optimizing usage in real time based on consumption patterns. Through Wiser HEMS, which                                               CH9
supports protocols like ZigBee, Wi-Fi, Matter, KNX, and Modbus, users can manage everything in one app. Key innovations include
electrification, where appliances intuitively adjust to schedules for up to 25% energy savings(1); digitalization, using AI-powered automation
to optimize usage; and decentralization, enabling homes to produce and store clean energy and integrate EVs.

Customer Success Story – JFK International Airport




     JFK Terminal One needed to become more resilient and sustainable. Their goal was to operate
     off-grid during power disruptions and meet strict New York climate laws. Schneider provided an
     integrated solution covering building automation, data center systems, and device-level controls.
     The microgrid solution at the terminal powers the equivalent of 3,570 homes annually using solar, fuel cells, and battery storage.
     This supports New York’s climate goals and stabilizes long-term energy costs. JFK is now the first airport transit hub in the region to
     achieve 100% operational resilience during outages.

     2.1.1.2.2 Contribution to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs)
     The 17 UN SDGs are focused on protecting the planet, alleviating poverty, and achieving worldwide peace and justice. The Schneider
     Sustainability Impact (SSI) and Schneider Sustainability Essentials (SSE) programs contribute to those goals, directly or indirectly, for all
     stakeholders in the Company’s value chain. Schneider Electric is an active promoter of the SDGs and a member of the UN Global Compact
     (UNGC), its Chairman having been a Board Member from 2018 to 2024. The Group discloses each year its communication on progress,
     and was one of the 850 participants in the UNGC Early Adopters program in 2022. The following mapping of the Group contribution by
     SDG and stakeholder was realized by reviewing all 169 targets and leveraging the SDG Compass tools.

      2.2 Sustainability statements | CSRD
      As an impact-driven company and an energy technology leader, Schneider Electric
      aims to deliver strong performance contributing positively across environmental,
      social, and governance dimensions. The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive
      (CSRD) represents a significant evolution in sustainability disclosures, and
      complements the long-standing Schneider Sustainability Impact (SSI), which has
      guided the Group's sustainability performance management for more than a decade.

      Since 2024, Schneider Electric took a further step in transparency    These efforts reﬂect the Group's broader objective: to continuously
      by reporting in line with the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting   elevate the transparency and integrity of its reporting.
      Directive (CSRD) and the European Sustainability Reporting
      Standards (ESRS). This report provides a deeper understanding of      This report describes how Schneider Electric identifies and
      how sustainability is embedded in Schneider Electric strategy,        manages its material sustainability topics, including
      operations, and long-term value creation model.                       decarbonization, circularity, resource efficiency, human rights,
                                                                            working conditions, responsible supply chain practices, and trust,
      Delivering robust and comparable sustainability information relies    among others. It also outlines how sustainability is embedded
      on strong data governance. Over the past years, the Group             within the Group’s value-creation model, risk-management
      enhanced its internal processes, strengthened cross-functional        processes, and long-term strategic planning.
      collaboration, and invested in improved systems to ensure the
      quality, completeness, and traceability of the data presented.

         Trust Charter, Schneider Electric’s Code of Conduct
         The Trust Charter (available in more than 40 languages on Schneider Electric’s website), acts as the Group’s Code of Conduct and
         demonstrates the Group’s commitment to ethics, safety, sustainability, quality, and cybersecurity. It powers all the interactions with
         stakeholders and all relationships with customers, shareholders, employees, and the communities Schneider Electric serves, in a
         meaningful, inclusive, and positive way. It serves as a compass, showing the true north in an ever more complex world. Trust is a
         foundational value of Schneider Electric, and it is core to its ESG commitments.
         Schneider Electric developed the Trust Charter, owned by the Group Risk Management team, with the support of various internal
         teams including Governance, Customer Satisfaction & Quality, Sustainability, Global Human Resources, Global Supply Chain, Global
         Finance, Global Marketing, and Corporate Citizenship. This document is made available to stakeholders through Schneider Electric’s
         website and is referenced within contractual relationships.
         All Schneider Electric employees are expected to comply with Schneider Electric’s Trust programs. They are based on management
         commitment which makes its pillars effective and on risk assessment which assists decision making, determining the risks to be
         treated and the priority to implement the treatment.
         Through its Trust programs, Schneider Electric aims to prevent, detect, and mitigate integrity risks including corruption, fraud,
         violation of human rights, health and safety, responsible workplace (including discrimination, harassment, and sexual harassment),
         anti-competitive practices, sanctions and export control, tax law, quality, cybersecurity, as well as data privacy and protection. The
         program design and operation are inﬂuenced by the Group’s risk profile, business model, organizational structure, and culture.
         Each section of the Trust Charter states clear Dos and Don’ts and provides clear references to relevant policies and procedures,
         which are adapted to meet local legal requirements when necessary. This Code of Conduct applies to everyone working at Schneider
         Electric or any of Schneider Electric’s subsidiaries. It is both an individual and collective responsibility to comply and respect laws
         and regulations, to apply Schneider Electric policies, and to uphold strong ethical principles to earn trust at all times.

      Material sustainability impacts, risks, and opportunities
      The table below presents the material impacts, risks, and opportunities for Schneider Electric in 2025, i.e. the “high level” Financial risks
      and the “high level” Impacts.

      The Group’s approach to sustainability is characterized by a forward-looking perspective. Hence, all impacts, risks, and opportunities were
      evaluated in the short- (current), medium- (2 – 5 years), and long-term (beyond 5 years).
      All material impacts are expected in the short and medium term, while long-term impacts are also expected in areas where the Group
      anticipates significant market changes that differ from near-term expectations, which is the case for the impacts related to climate change
      adaptation, climate change mitigation, energy, resources inﬂows, and resource outﬂows. These time horizons have been defined as per
      ESRS 1, paragraph 6.4 Definition of short-, medium- and long-term for reporting purposes.

Even though so far most of the identified material risks and potential negative impacts have not materialized in a substantial manner, the
Group recognizes sustainability is a shifting domain and works to continuously improve and adapt its strategy to maintain a robust business
model. It does so by constantly evaluating its resilience in relation to impacts and risks through the various assessments that have been
described previously in this section, including the ERM framework and Vigilance plan matrix, among others.

The effects of the material impacts, risks, and opportunities on the Company’s business model and strategy, along with the resulting
policies and actions that form part of the Group’s resilience strategy, are detailed in the relevant sections of this sustainability statement.

In the past, Schneider Electric’s transformational programs and strategic direction have evolved in response to sustainability issues, and
will continue to do so to anticipate significant changes in the market.

      Main decarbonization levers
      Based on the nature of the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from Schneider Electric’s activities across the three scopes, several
      decarbonization levers and key actions have been identified to mitigate climate change. The detailed description of these decarbonization
      levers, their impact towards the 2030 targets, and their foreseeable associated financial resources over the next 5 years are detailed in the
      sections below. Due to intrinsic uncertainties in modelling future GHG emissions, the current financial planning has been done from the
      perspective of the 2030 targets, while 2050 is beyond forecasting horizon. However, the Group anticipates that the nature of most
      decarbonization levers will be similar between 2030 and 2050, with very likely a bigger activation of these levers. It is also anticipated
      that technological innovation and improvements in carbon accounting granularity and accuracy will result in identifying new levers in the
      coming years. The Group will actively monitor progress in these fields. Lastly, regarding the Scope 3 target for 2030 specifically, the
      forecasting exercise reveals a possible gap to the target, due to the dependence on external factors such as the rate of decarbonization
      in the electricity grid and in the industrial sector. If the electricity grid were to decarbonize at a slower rate than what is anticipated in the
      modelled scenario, the Group would adapt its decarbonization strategy accordingly.

      The milestones of Schneider Electric’s Carbon Pledge are presented on the below visual with the key decarbonization levers. The Group
      has elaborated a comprehensive climate strategy of climate-related programs, that are shown on the next page and has made projections
      of the impacts of the main decarbonization levers.

      reduction since 2021 is largely due to energy efficiency initiatives,
      electrification of the Group’s on-site processes and ﬂeet, as well as
      the outstanding progress on sourcing more and more renewable
      electricity.

      On Scope 3, upstream emissions have decreased in 2025 by -5%
      as compared to 2024, and by -7% since 2021 (market-based), due
      to the reduction of volume of commodities being purchased, eco-
      design of offers, and the efforts of the decarbonization programs in
      the supply chain (e.g., Green Materials program which contributes
      to source materials with low carbon footprint, and The Zero
      Carbon Project which supports the decarbonization of Schneider
      Electric's top 1,000 suppliers). Downstream emissions, the majority
      of which come from the use of sold products, have decreased in
      2025 by -0.4% as compared to 2024, and by -12% since 2021.
      This is due to a combination of eco-design of offers with the

      Physical risks
      Schneider Electric employs a comprehensive process to assess physical risk financial effects, integrating scenario analysis (across five
      pathways) with the Group’s broader risk management strategy. This includes an ISO 22301-aligned program that maps substantive
      financial risks (asset destruction, profit loss) and ensures continuity from incident to recovery.
              Please refer the section on "Climate physical and transition risks" for more information on the assessment of climate
              physical risks.

In order to ensure there are no severe pitfalls for successfully
implementing the decarbonization actions, Schneider Electric has
looked into material locked-in GHG emissions in the activities of
the Group.

For Scopes 1 and 2, since there is no asset operated by Schneider
Electric that would represent more than 5% of the Group's
emissions, there is no key asset with material locked-in emissions
(indeed, the Group is using 5% as materiality threshold, as
suggested by the SBTi framework). However, the Group identified
some manufacturing sites with gas-intensive manufacturing
processes, and is actively looking for ways to electrify these
processes and there is no impediment to implement the
transition plan from this viewpoint.

​Simply put, Net-Zero means balancing the carbon the Group puts
                                                                                                                                                     CH9
into the atmosphere with the carbon it takes out, towards the point
when the planet stops heating up.

​Until then, the world keeps warming, which means preventing CO2
entering the atmosphere and helping reduce atmospheric
 CO2 today are critical to reducing peak warming and its
 consequences.

Schneider Electric believes that managing the Earth’s climate over
the coming years and decades is as important as managing it over
the coming centuries, and that successful climate mitigation
needs to focus both on short- and long-term time scales.

​To this end, Schneider Electric's strategy includes near-term
 climate milestones alongside long-term ones, aligned with science
and inclusive of the need to build the markets for Net-Zero.

In 2025, Schneider Electric’s portfolio addressing ongoing operational emissions includes three projects, each contributing to climate resilience,
community well-being, and ecosystems restoration:                                                                                                            IR

1. The improved cookstoves project in Embu County, Kenya, Hifadhi 1 (83,102 tCO2e) is mitigating deforestation through rural energy
    and agroforestry. Named “Hifadhi”, which means “to preserve” in Swahili, this project distributed 60,000 improved cookstoves in
                                                                                                                                                             CH1
    three districts in Embu County (Embu East, Embu North, Mbere South), located at the foot of Mount Kenya. Its main impact is that it
    decreases wood consumption by 60% compared to the traditional three-stone cookstove, as tests done by researchers at Kenyatta
    University in Nairobi have confirmed. This project will save 13,000 tons of wood and save more than 1 million tonnes of CO2e over the


                                                                                                                                                             C H 2 – S U S TA I N A B L E
    project’s life span of ten years. On the field, the project developer is Climate Pal, a joint venture between Carbon Manna Africa (40%),
    a Kenyan company, and EcoAct (60%) – now SE Advisory Services. In 2025, the project received an award from the Leuchtturm-
    Wettbewerbs der Stiftung Allianz für Entwicklung und Klima (Flagship-Competition for Climate Protection Projects).



                                                                                                                                                                 DEVELOPMENT




                                                                                                                                                             CH3



                                                                                                                                                             CH4



                                                                                                                                                             CH5



                                                                                                                                                             CH6
2. The Qori Q’oncha improved cookstoves diffusion program in Peru (38,629 tCO2e) is fighting deforestation and improving the health of
   families in the Andes. Started in 2016, the project is providing upfront financing to ITYF, a local NGO, to extend its efficient cookstoves
   project and provide communities with health and hygiene kits, and trainings. 30,000 households, among the poorest of Ayacucho and                         CH7
   Huancavelica, are impacted by this program. The project is cutting wood consumption by 60%, avoiding the emission of more than
   1 million tons of CO2e in the atmosphere over 14 years.
                                                                                                                                                             CH8



                                                                                                                                                             CH9




3. The mangrove restoration and coastal greenbelt protection project in the east coast of Aceh and North Sumatra Province,
   Indonesia, Yagasu 1 (11,769 tCO2e) is focusing on mangroves revitalising coastal villages with fishery and new businesses.
   Launched in 2011, the Livelihoods-Yagasu project restored mangrove forests, and as a result, increased the resilience of the local
   population in the face of extreme climate events. Between 2011 and 2014, Livelihoods-Yagasu project helped plant 18 million
   mangrove seedlings on 5,000 hectares to rebuild a natural mangrove barrier, that is essential to maintain life in these fragile areas.
   The 18 million trees planted will sequester more than 2 million tCO2e over 20 years. Additionally, this project generates new sources
   of economic income. Local villagers can now increase their revenues by selling the by-products of the mangroves such as fish,
   crabs, mollusks, and natural dyes that could be made from the parts of the mangrove tree.

energy consumption monthly through invoices using the EcoStruxure™ Resource Advisor software suite. The energy consumption of the

industrial buildings, and an average energy consumption of 70 kWh/sqm/year for its 30 logistics buildings.

      2.2.2.3.5 Resource Inﬂows and Outﬂows
      Resource inﬂows
      Overall total weight of products
      Schneider Electric reports the total weight of products by consolidating information from procurement spend. Schneider Electric organizes
      procurement spend by assigning a category code (CATs codes) to each group of material purchases (e.g., metal stamping parts, battery,
      semi-conductors, etc…). Available weights data for each category are used systematically. A complementary approach has been
      developed to calculate total global volume in the most accurate way recognizing that some extrapolation and assumptions are required.

      Volume and percentage of sustainably sourced biological content (wood)
      The below table shows Schneider Electric’s material resource inﬂow. Please note that, in Schneider Electric’s context, biological material is
      understood as wood (further details can be found in the ‘Methodology’ section below).

      Volume and percentage of recycled components
      There are two contexts in which Schneider Electric uses secondary recycled or reused materials in manufacturing. The first is responsible
      materials purchases (including thermoplastics, steel, aluminium), the second is through recycled lead, cardboard and paper purchases.
      The Group is working to expand the use of recycled materials and will add on additional recycled material purchases over time.

      The table below present the key metrics with regards to volume & percentage of recycled components.

      The year-over-year change was driven by improved data quality of the figures, notably on wood and on lead weights.

      Luminous volumes account for about 10% of total weight, which is driven by their product mix mainly composed of metals (lead batteries).

      from the recycled lead used by Luminous to manufacture lead-acid batteries.

      Action plan
      Collaborating with Fair Wage Network since 2022 allowed the
      Group to improve geographical coverage, develop a dynamic
      web-based living wage benchmark, and initiate an independent
      review and certification of the living wage gap analysis. Schneider
      Electric was certified in March 2024, by the Fair Wage Network,
      being qualified as a “Living Wage Employer” for a second
      consecutive time, valid until December 31, 2025. To measure
      compliance with the living wage, a gap analysis is conducted
      every year post salary review for all our Schneider Electric
      employees treated as permanent workforce. All employees
      employed by fully integrated entities, with open-ended or
      fixed-term contracts, whether full-time or part-time, are
      considered part of the permanent workforce.

      In 2025, living wage benchmarks were integrated into the Group’s
      “Fair Pay Simulator,” making it more accessible and user-friendly
      for the HR community. While the tool now includes living wage
      benchmarks data, its primary purpose remains to simulate
      compensation offers in a way that is market competitive and fair by
      preventing pay gap creation. It supports key HR processes such
      as promotions and salary adjustments.

      Schneider Electric in 2025. Focusing specifically on reported
      issues of discrimination, harassment, and sexual harassment, the
      Group received 1,500 potential violations. Of these, 893 were
      determined to be valid. Additionally, among the cases related to
      discrimination, harassment, and sexual harassment that were
      closed in 2025, 392 were substantiated following investigation, for
      which appropriate actions have been taken. All these elements are
      reviewed and analyzed by the Ethics & Compliance team to ensure
      an improvement on this matter and to ensure equal treatment for
      all within Schneider Electric.

      In 2021, a specific self-assessment questionnaire was developed,
      building on the experiences of on-site audits performed during
      previous years. Among the questions asked, the core ones aim to
      check whether the suppliers are compliant on mandatory subjects
      of labor, human rights, environment, and health and safety. The
      two main goals of this assessment are to help the supplier to reﬂect
      on its compliance to vigilance standards, and for Schneider
      Electric to identify whether on-site audits may be necessary.
      During 2025, 74 suppliers submitted answers.

                                                                             about 1,500 suppliers had been audited on-site, and 16 500+

                                                                             Electric to raise 1,700+ non-conformances ; we can observe this
                                                                             year a decrease of the overall ratio of Non Conformances per
                                                                             supplier compared to previous years.

                                                                             Out of these non-conformances, 192 are assessed as “top priority”
                                                                             and are given very specific attention during the re-audits of the
                                                                             suppliers.
                                                                             Schneider Electric’s objective is to close 100% of all types of non-
                                                                             conformances identified, whatever their priority level.

                                                                             Overall, the resolution of non-conformances identified since the
                                                                             program’s inception in 2017 has supported the improvement of the
                                                                             working conditions for an estimation of 400,000 employees. As
                                                                             example, correct minimum wages, safe working conditions,
                                                                             maximum working hours, overtime paid in line with the law.

  Key pillars of the Decent Work program include:                                                                                                      IR

 1. Employment               Employment opportunities should be available to all eligible, in a transparent, well-informed manner, and
    opportunities            without any charges, as a right. In case of any expense incurred by the worker towards obtaining
                             employment, the same should be reimbursed by the employer. The work should respect and uphold the                         CH1
                             dignity of employees and proactively create an environment to address and resolve modern slavery,
                             forced labor, and bonded labor. There should be a process to ensure no child is employed.


                                                                                                                                                       C H 2 – S U S TA I N A B L E
 2. Adequate earnings        Employment should be a source of economic independence and dignified living. The gradual decline of
    and productive work      industrial wages and the COVID-19 crisis have severely impacted the economic outlook of the workforce,
                             globally. Companies should review wage policies to ensure the affordability of a dignified living by the


                                                                                                                                                           DEVELOPMENT
                             workers. Additionally, employment should equip the workforce to improve current skill sets and knowledge
                             for future employability.

 3. Decent working           Excessive working hours is a legal violation, often accepted as “necessary”. It is generally connected with
    hours                    low industrial wages and used as an excuse to not provide appropriate wages. Companies should review
                                                                                                                                                       CH3
                             and remediate excessive hours and should align with the legal and/or international requirements.

 4. Stability and security   Employment should be a source of economic stability and peace of mind. Uncertainty of job security
    of work                  increases stress and makes the workforce vulnerable to abuse and hazardous working conditions. The                        CH4
                             problem has been exacerbated due to COVID-19-related job losses.

                                                                                                                                                       CH5
 5. Social dialogue and      Employees should have the right to engage with management and collectively put across their concerns
    workplace relations      and demands. Collective bargaining and freedom of association encourages workers to raise concerns in
                             a timely manner, acts as a barometer and early warning system to assess worker satisfaction, and reduces
                             worker vulnerability.                                                                                                     CH6



 6. Fair treatment in        Employment should be based on merit and the ability to do the job, and fair treatment should be extended                  CH7
    employment               to all employees. Differences in lifestyle, choices, etc., often become a source of discrimination,
                             victimization, and harassment. This curbs freedom of expression, hiding preferences, and creates mental
                                                                                                                                                       CH8
                             health challenges. Companies should ensure a workplace that accepts diversity and provides an inclusive
                             work environment.

 7. Safe work                Employment should result in economic independence and augment the ability to exercise a healthy and                       CH9
                             prosperous life. It should not result in ill-health, risk to well-being, or be a source of injury/misery.

 8. Social protection        Industrial wages are often not sufficient to provide adequate living standards. The problem is exacerbated
                             in cases of health emergencies. Social protection, provided by employers/governments, provides a much-
                             needed safety net from economic shock, descent into poverty, and vulnerability. Companies should ensure
                             that all employees have access to social security safety net.

 9. Purchasing practices     Purchasing practices and requirements significantly impact working conditions. They inﬂuence the working
                             culture of the supplier organization to meet customer requirements. The power of procurement can be a
                             strong driver for positive change to include decent work conditions as a prerequisite among the supply
                             chain partners, when balanced with other commercial criteria.

 10. Balancing work and      Family responsibilities disproportionately impact genders and result in unequal participation in economic
     family life             activities. Workplaces should strive to create a level playing field and provide all possible opportunities to
                             employees to participate in economic activities without compromising the family responsibilities, which
                             may require periods away from work (e.g., maternity, family care, ﬂexible hours, and adequate childcare).
                             The work environment should act as a leveler/equalizer and not augment the disparity.

injuries. The failure of a product, system, or solution may not only

Electric's customers, but it can also entail costs related to
product recall, result in new development expenditure, and
consume technical and economic resources, on top of brand or
reputational damage.

As part of the mission to deliver connected solutions that help
consumers manage energy consumption, from their homes to
electric vehicles, Schneider Electric processes data related to
lifestyle and usage patterns. In the unlikely event of a security
incident, unauthorized disclosure could impact consumer privacy
and trust. This is why data privacy and protection are core
priorities at Schneider Electric, supported by robust policies,
processes, and technologies designed to minimize risk and uphold
the highest standards of privacy and compliance. Schneider
Electric cybersecurity and data protection policies, processes, and
measures are designed to minimize the likelihood of the risk to
consumers’ private life materializing.

      on risks linked to the Group's third-party relationships. This
      capability will support the business into getting more visibility on
      risks (covering compliance, finance, cybersecurity, environment
      and human rights), and making informed decisions.

      Schneider Electric determines the total weight of products and
      related sustainability indicators using a structured, data-driven
      methodology that consolidates procurement, plant-level, and
      supplier information across the Group. The reporting boundary
      includes all direct purchases of raw materials, components, and
      packaging, while excluding subcontracting, services, and
      software.

      Overall total weight of products
      Product weight is calculated by converting procurement spend into
      physical volumes using as much actual weight data that is
      available. Approximately 80% of raw materials and fabricated
      components are covered by plant-reported weights. For categories
      without direct volume data, the Group applies category-level
      analyses using quantities and unit-of-measure data to derive
      weight-to-spend ratios. The ratios are then multiplied by total
      spend to assess full coverage. Electronics weights are derived by
      aggregating known part weights, removing outliers, grouping
      comparable families, and applying gram-per-euro ratios to total
      category spend. This multi-source approach ensures 100%
      coverage while progressively reducing reliance on estimates
      through expanded data capture and supplier engagement.

          Beyond CSRD
      At Schneider Electric, sustainability is central to its strategy. As the world faces urgent
      social and environmental challenges, including biodiversity loss and climate change,
      companies must take decisive actions to be agents of change. Social and environmental
      innovation are core to Schneider Electric's purpose.


      As an Energy Tech leader, Schneider Electric role is to act as a      • Social and Human progress: ensuring that the transition
      catalyst for progress at scale - not only for the Group but for its     creates real opportunities. Access to energy, skills development,
      industry, its customers, its territories, and the communities it        economic inclusion, and the ability for everyone to grow
      engages with:                                                           professionally and personally, while bringing well-being and
      • Technological progress: scaling the energy transition by              caring back to the center.
        putting technology, data and innovation at the core
      • Environmental progress: contributing in a measurable way to
        climate action and resource preservation, by addressing
        structural causes rather than symptoms alone.

2.3.3.6.4 Group policy                                                         For more details, see Chapter 3, section 3.2.4 Key risks
                                                                               and opportunities on page 371.
Schneider Electric’s export control approach is articulated around
its mission to provide education, advisory, business operations
support, and enforcement of the Export Control Policy and
strategy. The policy outlines Schneider's commitment to prevent
the unauthorized export of goods, services, technologies, and
information that could pose risks to national security, international
trade, or other regulatory concerns. The roles and responsibilities
of businesses, functions, and employees to ensure export control
compliance are clearly defined. The responsibilities include
designating individuals or teams responsible for overseeing export
control activities and implementing necessary controls. The policy,
signed by the Group Chief Executive Officer, sets the tone from the
top, and is applicable to all Schneider Electric employees.

As stated in its Trust Charter, Anti-Corruption Policy, Competition Law Policy, and various other policies, Schneider
Electric is committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations, such as the OECD’s Convention on
Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions, the US Foreign Corrupt Practices
Act (FCPA), the UK Bribery Act, the French Sapin II law, and the various antitrust laws and competition rules globally.

Schneider Electric has a zero tolerance policy with regard to corruption and breaches of competition laws and considers
that “doing the right thing” is a key value-creation driver for all its stakeholders. This commitment materialized through
strong and continuously developing programs such as its Anti-Corruption Compliance program (part of its Trust program,
see section 2.2.4.1 Zero tolerance for corruption on page 247), and its Competition Law program (see section
2.3.3.4 Compliance with competition law on page 310).                                                                            Business

The French Competition Authority issued on October 29, 2024 a decision to sanction several companies concerning the
electrical distribution activities in France, including Schneider Electric for a EUR 207 million penalty considering that the
pricing autonomy of some distributors in the French market had been limited by Schneider Electric, in breach of
competition rules.

Schneider Electric strongly disagrees with the conclusion of the French Competition and has appealed the decision in
front of the Paris Appeal Court. For more information, please see Note 22.2 "Contingent liabilities" page 531.

      2.4.2.2 Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) correspondence table
      Climate change has been clearly identified as crucial to both Schneider Electric’s internal and external stakeholders during the various
      materiality assessments that took place in 2014, 2017, 2020 and 2024. Overall, transformations linked to climate change are a source of
      opportunities for Schneider Electric, the main risk being to fail leading by example and thereby lose traction with customers, investors, new
      talents, and collaborators in the Company. Concrete climate-related programs to either grab opportunities or mitigate risks are deployed
      every 3 to 5 years with the Schneider Sustainability Impact (SSI) programs and complement the Group’s Net-Zero Commitment. Schneider
      Electric presents below its main climate-related disclosures in line with TCFD recommendations.

                                                        even with mitigation efforts, the IPCC is highly confident that climate change will

                                                                  distribution centers, and large offices. The IMS includes compliance with ISO

                                                                  periodic audits, either externally by Bureau Veritas every three years or internally

targets.                                               The Group has launched several concrete programs aiming at either directly or
                                                       indirectly reducing GHG emissions, under the Climate and Resources pillars of its
                                                       2025 strategy. These programs are presented under the SSI and SSE 2021 – 2025
                                                       programs on pages 79 to 89. These programs cover the performance of the
                                                       Group’s operations (such as energy efficiency, renewable electricity procurement,
                                                       ﬂeet electrification), suppliers (such as The Zero Carbon Project, green materials or
                                                       sustainable packaging) and customers (SF6-free alternative offers, CO2 savings
                                                       and avoidance quantification on customers’ end thanks to EcoStruxure™). As the
                                                       2021-2025 sustainability chapter is coming to an end, the Group is setting out to
                                                       announce the new set of 2030 sustainability targets. More details can be found in
                                                       section 2.1.3 Introducing Schneider Electric’s 2030 sustainability ambition on
                                                       page 92.

                                                         The overall performance of the SSI represents 20% of the short-term incentives for
                                                         more than 80,000 employees worldwide (collective share). The Carbon Emission
                                                         Reduction Targets, impact 25% of the long-term incentives (LTI) for 4,500+
                                                         grantees, including 3,000+ top leaders.

                                                         The Group is incorporating internal pricing systems, with purposes to inform the
                                                         Group’s climate strategy and incentivize low-carbon decisions. Carbon prices are
                                                         used in climate risk assessments to test how resilient the Group’s activities are
                                                         under different carbon pricing and climate scenarios. Under certain scenarios,
                                                         there is no value attached to carbon, while in aggressive Net-Zero scenarios, the
                                                         price could be up to several hundreds of euros. More details can be found in the
                                                         table “Internal carbon pricing” of section 2.2.2.1.5 Investment and resources on
                                                         page 141.

                                                         Schneider Electric is a signatory of the Business Ambition for 1.5°C initiative aimed
                                                         at setting GHG emissions reduction targets in line with the global effort to limit
                                                         warming to 1.5°C.

      Recommended                  CDP Corporate and              Brief description (please refer to CDP Corporate response and other sections of this
      Disclosure                   URD 2025 references            Universal Registration Document for further details)

                                                                  In August 2022, Schneider Electric was one of the first companies to see its GHG
                                                                  reduction targets validated by the SBTi, in alignment with its “Corporate Net-Zero
                                                                  Standard” published in October 2021. As part of its Net-Zero commitment, the
                                                                  Group has defined mid and long-term targets. As part of its 2050 SBTi targets, the
                                                                  Group is committed to be Net-Zero across its entire value chain by 2050, which
                                                                  means that the Group aims to reduce its 2021 footprint by an absolute 90% by
                                                                  2050 and neutralize residual emissions with high-quality carbon removal credits.

                                                                  The group aims to :
                                                                  • By 2030, reduce value chain emissions by 25% and be “Net-Zero ready” in
                                                                    operations by neutralizing all residual operational emissions with removals.
                                                                  • By 2050, reduce value chain emissions by 90% and reach Net-Zero CO2
                                                                    emissions by neutralizing all residual emissions with removals.

      The indicators below concern all entities where Schneider Electric has operational control, and integrated in the Group for more than
      two years. This scope differs from the CSRD scope presented in the section 2.2.1.3 Basis for preparation on page 124.

      Within the Group perimeter, given the complexity to obtain robust and meaningful data, in particular for small leased offices, estimated
      coverage indicators are provided for each reporting table. All Group industrial and logistics sites, in addition to certain major tertiary sites
      are covered. As per the Group’s Environmental Policy, all industrial and logistics sites with more than 50 people and tertiary sites with more
      than 500 people must be ISO 14001 certified within 2 years after their acquisition or creation. A difference can, therefore, be noted with
      respect to the scope of financial consolidation.

(1) Waste reduction measures specific, targeted projects which reduce/avoid waste. Examples of waste reduction projects include creating a closed-loop system for

    not count as waste reduction.

    total non-hazardous waste generated and waste reduced. The Group’s waste recovery percentage without waste reduction is: 96.2%, 97.1%, 96.5%, 95.9% for 2025,
    2024, 2023, 2022 respectively.
(3) ‘Schneider Electric expectations’ for hazardous waste means: 1) Waste meets/exceeds all local legal requirements for handling/treatment, and either 2a) waste is
    neutralized of its hazardous nature, or b) waste is handled/treated using the feasibly best available technique which provides the most environmentally beneficial
    impact.

      (1) In 2025, Schneider Electric recalculated its 2021 base-year GHG inventory (Scopes 1, 2 and 3) to reﬂect material methodological updates, primarily in Scope 3
          Category 11 (use of sold products), improved alignment with industry standards and practice, and harmonization of organizational scope and other methodological
          elements. Targets remain unchanged, with only the absolute baseline and corresponding 2030 target levels recalculated.
      (2) All Schneider Electric sites and all major non-integrated entities are included in this table starting in 2024, resulting in 100% site coverage. In prior years, major
          non-integrated entities were excluded from Group results in this table
      (3) Scope 2 emissions are quantified with the market-based methodology and the location-based methodology, following GHG Protocol Scope 2 guidance, and the results
          from both approaches are disclosed. Values calculated with market-based and location-based methodologies should not be added. Market-based electricity
          emissions are calculated using subnational factors for the US and Canada, residual electricity emissions factors for European countries, and average country emission
          factors for other countries. Location-based Scope 2 electricity emissions on energy reporting perimeter are equal to 291,877 tCO2e (audited value), and 405,793 tCO2e
          on total Group perimeter (audited value). Total Scope 2 (location-based) emissions is 409,343 tCO2e (audited value). Total Scope 1 and 2 (location-based) CO2
          emissions (energy, vehicles, and SF6 emissions in tCO2e) on full perimeter are equal to 509,651 tCO2e (audited value).
      (4) The CO2 emissions linked to energy consumption for sites outside the energy reporting perimeter are considered estimates for two reasons: on the one hand, energy
          consumption and corresponding CO2 emissions of these sites are estimated (instead of being collected from meters and invoices, energy consumption are based on
          site surface and average energy intensity of sites per region from the energy reporting perimeter); on the other hand, the indirect emissions are calculated on the
          conversion factors per country and not with supplier-specific data.
      (5) Scope 3 upstream emissions can be quantified with the market-based methodology and the Group has completed a dual reporting in 2025 to represent this impact.
          The market based impacts were driven by a purchase of sustainable aviation fuel, the incorporation of reduction due to suppliers having zero Scope 2 emissions and
          the impact of Scope 2 market-based reductions on upstream Scope 3 electricity-related emissions. More details can be found in “Inclusion of market-based accounting
          approach” p.153, section 2.2.2.1.7
      (6) In 2024 the methodology has changed, leading to significant changes as compared to previous year.
      (7) Prior to 2023, this category was meant to capture greenhouse gas emissions (CH4 and N2O emissions) generated from renewable electricity produced with biomass.
      (8) These emissions correspond to products sold by Schneider Electric during the year of reporting and cumulated over their lifetime. These emissions are attributable to
          electricity consumption of products, either due to internal consumption or due to heat dissipation (Joule effect). The GHG emissions from electricity considered are
          forward-looking during the lifetime of products, based on a scenario from the International Energy Agency (IEA) that factors in the future decarbonization of the grids.
      (9) Avoided CO2 emissions are calculated for sales of the reporting year and cumulated over the offers’ lifetime. Emissions are calculated as the difference between
          emissions with Schneider Electric’s offer and emissions in the reference situation. The methodology distinguishes “saved” and “avoided” emissions: saved CO2
          emissions correspond to brownfield sales that enable reduction of global CO2 emissions compared to previous years, while avoided CO2 emissions correspond to
          greenfield sales that enable a limitation of the increase of global emission. When new methodologies are developed during the reporting year, CO2 saved and avoided
          from those offers is quantified for sales that occurred since 2018 and counted fully in the performance of the reporting year. In addition, methodologies are continuously
          improved, leading potentially to some adjustments with retroactive impact. In 2025, there has been no update to methodology. However, out of the 183.3 MTCO2e
          saved and avoided in 2025, 90.1 MT (49.1%) came from new offers, which includes their 2021-2024 backdated performance.

3.1 Introduction                                                                                                                                    IR




                                                                                                                                                    CH1
When introducing Schneider Electric’s approach to risk management, it is important to distinguish between Enterprise Risk Management
(ERM) and Duty of vigilance (DoV).
                                                                                                                                                    CH2
Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) is the Group’s framework for identifying and managing risks that could affect its objectives,
reputation, or assets. It ensures a proactive, coordinated approach across all areas.




                                                                                                                                                    CH3 – RISK MANAGEMENT
Duty of Vigilance (DoV) is a legal requirement to identify, prevent, and reduce risks related to human rights, health and safety, and
environmental impacts in the Company’s operations and supply chain.

While ERM focuses on protecting the organization as a whole, DoV centers on safeguarding people and the planet, reﬂecting a
responsibility to act ethically and sustainably. Together, these frameworks reinforce Schneider Electric’s commitment to robust governance,
responsible business conduct, and long-term resilience.



                                                                                                                                                    AT S C H N E I D E R E L E C T R I C

3.2 Enterprise Risk Management
                                                                                                                                                    CH4
3.2.1 Risk management scope
The Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework is designed                Acquired companies are integrated progressively into the Group            CH5
to cover the Group, defined as the Schneider Electric SE parent           internal control and risk management systems.
company and the subsidiaries over which it exercises exclusive
control.                                                                                                                                            CH6

3.2.4 Key risks and opportunities                                                                                                                   IR



Principal risks                                                                                                                                     CH1

The Group risk inventory is organized in three categories and includes 21 key risks identified.
The key risks selected and presented below are the risks considered by the Group as specific to its business and identified as having the           CH2
potential to affect its activity, its image, its financial situation, its results, or the achievement of its objectives.




                                                                                                                                                    CH3 – RISK MANAGEMENT
However, the Group may be exposed to other non-specific risks, or risks of which it may not be aware, or risks of which it may be
underestimating the potential consequences, or other risks that may not have been considered by the Group as being likely to have a
material adverse impact on the Group, its business, financial condition, reputation, or outlook. In each category, risks are assessed in terms
of potential impact for the Group according to three levels (red, orange, and green), with red being the most likely to affect the Group. The
assessment is the result of the process performed as part of the overall risk management mechanism described in section 3.2.3.3 ERM
core processes for risk identification and management on page 367. The impact considered for the assessment is the potential net



                                                                                                                                                    AT S C H N E I D E R E L E C T R I C
impact which corresponds to the potential gross impact (financial/ human/ legal/ reputation), after having taken into consideration the
current mitigation measures, as well as the probability of occurrence of the risk. The assessment by Schneider Electric of this level of
materiality may be changed at any time, in particular should new facts, whether external or specific to the Group, come to light.
The identification and mitigation of the Group’s key risks can reveal opportunities for growth, enabling strategic decision making and
ﬂexibility to move ahead with speed.

                                                                         Global Human Rights Policy
                                                                         This policy’s objective is to define our position on human rights
                                                                         along the value chain. It also serves as a set of rules applicable
                                                                         to its daily operations for Schneider Electric and its employees.
                                                                         The list of human rights presented in this policy is not exhaustive.
                                                                         A human right should be defined as a right that aims to protect
                                                                         human dignity and that must be guaranteed for all.

                                                                         The Supplier Code of Conduct covers the full range of
                                                                         expectations towards suppliers, from human rights, ethical
                                                                         conduct, environmental management, occupational health and
                                                                         safety, material and resource use, engagement with sub-suppliers,
                                                                         and access to remedy.

An independent and balanced governance structure                                                                                                                                  IR

The Board of Directors of Schneider Electric SE is 92% independent and seeks to ensure a gender balance and broad diversity in terms of
skills, experience, nationality, and age. The Board of Directors constantly reviews its composition and searches for complementary profiles
                                                                                                                                                                                  CH1
in line with the skill set highlighted by its skill matrix and the challenges of the Company. The current governance structure which separates
the offices of Chairman of the Board of Directors and Chief Executive Officer has been in force since 2023. As part of this governance
structure, the term of office of Chairman of the Board of Directors is exercised by Mr. Jean-Pascal Tricoire, and that of Chief Executive
                                                                                                                                                                                  CH2
Officer by Mr. Olivier Blum who was appointed by the Board of Directors on November 1, 2024.

                              Skills                      Definition

                              Public company management   Directors with experience in executive leadership positions of public companies. These positions
                                                          include industry CEOs as well as other top executive positions (e.g., CEO of private companies,
                                                          CFO, COO) and top management roles (regional or divisional leadership).
                              Corporate finance           Directors who have gained experience in banking, investments, restructuring, or M&A. Also, those
                                                          high-level executives with responsibilities for financial management (e.g., CEO, CFO).
                              Accounting, audit & risk    Directors from an auditing, or finance role (e.g., financial reporting responsibilities). Also, expertise
                                                          in risk management gained from subject matter expertise or responsibility for corporate risk
                                                          management.
                              International markets       Directors who have spent a large portion of their career in, or have been directly responsible for,
                                                          foreign markets.
                              Industry knowledge          Directors who have gained experience in energy, electricity, and automation sectors.
                              Employee perspective &      Directors who are also employees of the Group and have gained a deep and inside knowledge of
                              knowledge of the Group      the Group.



       Core Skills
                              Digital & software          Directors who have gained technical or managerial experience directly in information technology,
                                                          cybersecurity, digitization, software, data, artificial intelligence, and innovative technologies in
                                                          relevant industries.
                              Environment/Climate         To join the Schneider Board, all directors need to demonstrate during their recruitment process a
                                                          strong commitment as well as a good understanding of environmental and climate topics. In this
                                                          skills are highlighted directors who have made very significant contributions to either sustainability
                                                          in business, climate change, or have important notoriety for promoting sustainable business in the
                                                          wider economy. This skill does include technical expertise such as experience in innovative green
                                                          technologies.
                              Social                      Directors who have gained experience and knowledge in social matters, and notably Human
                                                          Resources/Human Capital Management.
                                                          This also include former CEOs of public companies who have gained for a long period of time
                                                          expertise from responsibility, management, and supervision of social matters at the highest level.
                              Governance, law, ethics &   Directors with advanced and relevant legal qualification or experience in a corporate legal, or
                              compliance                  corporate governance setting, direct career exposure to relevant regulators, or governmental
                                                          organizations.
                                                          Also includes Directors who have a proven track record contributing to ethical business practices
                                                          and governance.
